newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria beefs up security on eve of elections.
newsitem.headline: Algeria beefs up security on eve of elections.

text.p: Algeria's armed forces beefed up security in the capital on Wednesday, a day before millions of Algerians vote in the first general election in five years of violence and bloodshed.

Heavily armed troops and police, backed by armoured troop carriers, increased roadblocks at the entrances of Algiers and in some streets near the city centre where Moslem rebels have been active in the past.
Armed plainclothes police deployed at polling stations but witnesses said their presence was less obtrusive than during the presidential election of November 1995.
The stepped-up security follows a bombing campaign in Algiers by suspected Moslem rebels in which 22 people were killed and 120 wounded. The last of three explosions targeting buses was on Monday.
No major rebel attacks have been reported since.
State-run radio repeated on Wednesday an Interior Ministry statement urging civilians to report all suspicious vehicles or packages at bus stops and on crowded streets.
The authorities earlier this week ordered all weekly markets and some schools to close until after the election. An old ban on parking cars in busy streets was also reinforced.
Voters queued at some government buildings to collect their election cards but traffic in Algiers was lighter than usual on a cloudy and windy but warm spring day.

Members of the security forces ended voting on Wednesday in early balloting designed to allow them to guard the polls, while Nomads in remote areas in the south of the vast country continued to vote at mobile ballot boxes.
Nearly 17 million Algerians are eligible to choose from more than 7,700 candidates representing 39 political parties for the 380-seat National Assembly (lower house).

The government of President Liamine Zeroual says the poll is key to resolving the country's civil strife which began when the authorities cancelled general elections in January 1992 which the now outlawed radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win.
An estimated 60,000 people have been killed since.

Two staunch anti-Islamist newspapers warned voters on Wednesday against giving the two legal Islam-oriented parties a substantial representation in the lower house, while the authorities called for a high turnout.
Under the headline "The spectre of December 1991", Le Matin daily said moderate Islamists of the Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) and Nahda parties were already "singing the victory song".
"If Islamists win tomorrow, it will be back to 1991," Le Matin said.
El Assil daily said the MPS, led by veteran Islamist leader Mahfoud Nahnah, was trying to "infiltrate democracy" and steal a win for Islamists.
"Public opinion realised a long time ago that the 'Islamisation of democracy' is a boy-ish attempt that will disappear like dust," El Assil said.
Analysts expect MPS to do well but they tip the National Democratic Rally (RNP), which groups government supporters, to emerge as the leading party in parliament.
Other main parties contesting the ballot include the Socialist Forces Front of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
A new proportional representation law virtually guarantees that at least four or five parties will be represented in parliament, with little chance of a single party holding an absolute majority.
